title: Malaysia Renewable Energy Integration into Grid: Challenges
abstract: Malaysia grapples with balancing rapid renewable growth against grid stability, as experts warn of hidden bottlenecks and costly upgrades.
body:
2026-05-05

## Current Grid Capacity
The national grid, operated by Tenaga Nasional Berhad, has a peak capacity of 30,000 MW, of which 5,200 MW is dedicated to renewable sources. By 2025, renewable penetration reached 18% of total generation, a figure that has outpaced the 12% target set in the 2024 Energy Master Plan. Analysts note that the rapid increase in solar and wind farms has stretched the transmission network, creating voltage fluctuations that can trigger rolling blackouts if not addressed.

## Integration Challenges
One of the primary obstacles is the lack of flexible interconnection points. Dr. Ahmad Zain, senior energy analyst at the Malaysian Energy Institute, explained that many new solar parks are located in the east coast, far from the main transmission corridors that feed the capital region. “The distance creates losses and limits the ability to dispatch power when demand spikes,” he said. In addition, the grid’s protection schemes were designed for conventional synchronous generators and are not optimized for inverter‑based resources. This mismatch can lead to protection mis‑coordination during fault events.

The second challenge is the variability of renewable output. Wind farms in the west coast produce up to 70% of their capacity during monsoon season, but drop to 20% in the dry months. Solar farms in the south peak between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., leaving a gap in supply that must be filled by gas turbines. The cost of maintaining these backup units has risen, with the average fuel price projected to increase by 8% in 2026, according to the Ministry of Energy’s latest forecast.

## Policy and Regulatory Landscape
The government has introduced a feed‑in tariff of RM 0.12 per kWh for solar projects above 5 MW, but the tariff is set to phase out by 2028. The Energy Commission has also mandated that all new renewable projects must connect to the grid within 12 months of commissioning, a rule that has accelerated deployment but also pressured the transmission system. In a recent briefing, Minister of Energy, Datuk Seri Mohd Azhar, stated that the Ministry is working on a “grid upgrade roadmap” that includes the installation of 1,200 MW of high‑voltage direct current (HVDC) links by 2030.

The regulatory framework still lacks a clear mechanism for compensating grid operators for the ancillary services that renewable plants provide. As a result, many developers are reluctant to invest in storage solutions, which could otherwise smooth out supply peaks and troughs. The Energy Commission’s draft amendment to the Transmission Code, expected to be released in July, aims to introduce a market for frequency response services.

## Future Outlook
Looking ahead, the Malaysian Energy Institute projects that renewable penetration could reach 30% by 2030 if the current growth trajectory continues. However, the Institute warns that without significant grid investment, the risk of widespread outages will increase. The Institute’s scenario analysis shows that a 15% increase in transmission capacity could reduce the probability of blackouts from 4% to 1% over the next decade.

Industry stakeholders are calling for a coordinated approach that includes investment in smart grid technologies, such as real‑time monitoring and automated fault isolation. The National Grid Operator has already piloted a 50 MW microgrid in the Klang Valley that uses battery storage to buffer solar output, a project that is slated for expansion in 2027.

In conclusion, Malaysia’s ambition to become a renewable energy leader is tempered by the technical and regulatory challenges that accompany rapid deployment. The next few years will be critical in determining whether the country can balance growth with reliability, or whether the grid will become a bottleneck that slows progress.
